newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman party, rivals deadlocked in Zagreb vote.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman party, rivals deadlocked in Zagreb vote.

text.p: An opposition coalition was running neck and neck with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist party in elections for the city assembly of the capital Zagreb, preliminary returns showed on Monday.

Tudjman refused to recognise an earlier opposition victory in Zagreb regional elections in 1995, imposing a provisional mayoralty in a move that raised questions about the quality of democracy in the former Yugoslav republic.

With 267 of the capital's 615 polling stations reporting, Tudjman's HDZ party had 36 percent compared with 24 percent for the Social Democrats (SDP) and 12 percent for their allies, the Social Liberals (HSLS).

Croatians voted for municipal and county assemblies across the country on Sunday and pre-election polls indicated the SDP and HSLS, riding economic grievances, would challenge the HDZ in the more important large cities.

Early unofficial returns on voting for 21 county assemblies released by state television showed the HDZ, or Croatian Democratic Union, cruising to easy re-election in most of them including the rural belt around Zagreb.

Serbs in the former rebel enclave of Eastern Slavonia took part in a Croatian election for the first time. But voting in the region, now under transitional U.N. administration, was extended to Monday to make up for initial technical delays.
Final unofficial results in the elections were not due before later on Monday.

Totals for Eastern Slavonia, where Serbs were expected to back an ethnic party bloc to protect minority rights after the enclave reverts to central Croatian authority this summer, will not be available until later in the week.
Zagreb was the grand prize in the elections because it has a third of Croatia's population and controls almost half of the productive economy as well as a powerful patronage machine.
SDP and HSLS leaders said they had seen more comprehensive results than released by HDZ-controlled state television confirming that they had beaten the ruling party as in 1995.
"(In) Zagreb, the opposition coalition has scored a convincing victory, thus confirming the people's will of 1995," said Bozo Kovacevic, a member of the HSLS leadership.
Zdravko Tomac, deputy leader of the SDP, said: "I expect those who win will be allowed to take over the city and the Zagreb Crisis (of 1995-96) will not be repeated."
Tudjman dissolved the new opposition-dominated council in April 1996 after a long political deadlock that ensued after he vetoed a local change of power on "national security" grounds.
The president did not comment directly on Zagreb's early returns but said on state television that the HDZ was ready to cooperate with parties backing a similar programme.
He said the overall election outcome "confirms we are the central, strongest party in Croatian history... Anyone who is against the HDZ is against sovereign Croatia".
The HDZ has been criticised for an authoritarian style of rule and contempt for opposition. Hundreds of international observers came to help ensure voting was free and fair.
Diplomats say Croatia must demonstrate an unequivocal commitment to pluralism or it will have a hard time qualifying for coveted links with the European Union.

Voting in Eastern Slavonia began in chaos and confusion after ballot forms were sent to the wrong locations and voter registration lists turned up incomplete. Polling at more than half the 171 stations was delayed for hours.

The region's transitional U.N. administration (UNTAES), scrambling to rectify the damaging setback, later said all adult Serbs with Croatian citizenship papers could cast ballots even if their name was not on lists.
UNTAES also decided to reopen balloting booths on Monday from 10 a.m. (0800 gmt) to 7 p.m. (1700 gmt).

Analysts say at least a quarter of the enclave's 150,000 Serbs will probably flee to Serbia after the elections, fearing Tudjman's security guarantees will not restrain vengeful Croat war refugees who will soon return to reclaim their homes.
It was independent Croatia's fifth election and its first since the end of war with separatist minority Serbs touched off by its move to independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
The HDZ relied heavily on Tudjman's enduring charisma as "Father of the Nation" in the latest election campaign.
His party has lost popularity over alleged corruption and insensitivity to Croats who have fallen on financial hard times as the formerly socialist economy has been privatised.
